d.title: What recurrence costs, stated as two numbers
d.caption: An RNN's two costs are the same fact from different directions. Information from position 1 reaches position T through **T sequential steps**, so the path length is O(T) and the signal decays along it (3.2). And because step t needs step t−1's output, nothing can be computed in parallel — training time scales with sequence length regardless of how much hardware you own.

d.title: Three projections of the same input
d.caption: Q, K and V are three different linear views of the identical input sequence — which is what 'self' attention means. The division of labour is worth stating: the **query** asks what this position is looking for, the **key** advertises what each position offers, and the **value** is what actually gets copied once a match is scored.

d.title: Running it: the four shapes that have to line up
d.caption: Almost every self-attention bug is a shape or a transpose. The scores matrix is T×T and **must** be square — if it is not, Q and K have been multiplied the wrong way round. And the softmax goes over the **last** axis, the keys: over the wrong axis it still runs, still returns the right shape, and produces a weighted average over the queries instead, which is meaningless.

d.title: A property of the output: every position is a convex combination
d.caption: Each output row is a weighted average of value vectors with weights summing to one, so it lies inside the **convex hull** of the values — attention can only interpolate what is already there, never extrapolate beyond it. That is why the feed-forward network matters so much (4.4): it is the part of the block that can produce something new.

d.title: What the T x T matrix costs, in memory
d.caption: The scores matrix is quadratic in sequence length, and the arithmetic becomes hostile quickly: at 32,768 tokens with 8 heads in fp32 it is **34.36 GB** for a single sequence — more than most GPUs hold, for one example. O(1) path length and quadratic memory are the same fact, and every efficient-attention paper is an attempt to keep the first while escaping the second.

state: one sequence, more than a GPU

d.title: Three ways to tell a transformer where it is
d.caption: Self-attention is permutation-equivariant (3.8), so position must be supplied. The three approaches differ in what they encode and how far they extrapolate: sinusoidal and learned encodings give each position an **absolute** identity, while RoPE rotates Q and K so that only the **relative** offset survives the dot product — which is why it generalises past the training length far better.
cells: a bag of tokens, at any length

d.title: Two thirds of a transformer block is the feed-forward network
d.caption: At the standard d_model = 512, d_ff = 2048 configuration, the two linear layers hold **67%** of the block's parameters against attention's 33%. That reframes what a transformer is: a stack of per-token MLPs with an attention mechanism routing information between them. It also explains where efficiency work goes — mixture-of-experts replaces the FFN, not the attention, because that is where the parameters are.

d.title: The feed-forward network is where a position is transformed
d.caption: It is applied **independently at every position** with the same weights — so it is a 1×1 convolution over the sequence, and it is the only part of the block that can produce a value outside the convex hull of its inputs (4.2). The 4× expansion gives the non-linearity room to work: squeeze it to 1× and the block loses most of its capacity.

nodes.label: GELU
nodes.sub: the only non-linearity in the block

d.title: Pre-norm and post-norm put the LayerNorm on different sides
d.caption: The original paper put the norm **after** the residual addition; every large model since puts it **before** the sublayer. The reason is the gradient path: with pre-norm the residual stream is an unnormalised identity from the loss to the embedding, so deep stacks train without a warmup crutch. Post-norm needs careful warmup and still destabilises past a few dozen layers.

d.title: The KV cache, and why generation is memory-bound
d.caption: Without a cache, generating token n re-attends over all n−1 previous tokens from scratch — quadratic work for a linear output. The cache stores each position's K and V once, so each new token costs one step. The consequence is the defining fact of LLM serving: generation reads a large cache per token and does almost no arithmetic, so it is **memory-bandwidth-bound**, not compute-bound.

d.title: The translation model, as it is assembled
d.caption: Read it bottom-up. The encoder stack sees the whole source at once; the decoder stack is causal over the target and additionally **cross-attends** to the encoder's output, which is the one connection between the two halves and the thing to inspect when a translation is fluent but wrong (§04).

items.label: Cross-attention
items.sub: queries from the target, keys from the source

d.title: Training it: one forward pass for the whole target
d.caption: This is the transformer's decisive advantage over an RNN decoder. Because the causal mask prevents any position seeing the future, the **entire** target sequence can be processed in one parallel pass — every position predicting its own next token simultaneously. The same model at inference must go one token at a time, which is why training is fast and generation is not.

nodes.label: Fast to train, slow to generate

d.title: Generation, and the three things that must match training
d.caption: Generation re-enters the model with its own output, so any mismatch with training shows up as fluent nonsense. The three to check are the **special tokens** (start the decoder with the same BOS it was trained with), the **shift** (the input is the target shifted right by one), and the **stop** condition (generate until EOS or a length cap, or it runs forever).

nodes.label: Forward, take the last position
nodes.sub: its logits are the next token

nodes.label: Stop at EOS, or a cap

d.title: Reading the cross-attention as a diagnostic
d.caption: Cross-attention is the only place the target looks at the source, so its weights are a soft alignment and are genuinely informative here — unlike the attention-is-not-attribution caution of ML 9.3, because this attention **is** the information path. A diagonal band means the model is translating in order; a column that attracts every target position usually means a source token the model cannot handle.

d.title: What to check when it will not train
d.caption: Every row produces a model that runs and learns nothing, so none of them raises. The order is by how often it is the cause — and the first two account for most of it, because both are silent and both are about the mask.

d.title: What each architecture assumes about its input
d.caption: This is the honest basis for choosing, and it is about **structure** rather than power. A CNN assumes locality and translation invariance; an RNN assumes order and that recent context matters most; a transformer assumes nothing about structure and so must be told position explicitly and shown far more data.
cells: quadratic memory, and needs more data

d.title: Parameter cost, at comparable widths
d.caption: The comparison that matters is per-layer at the same hidden width. The LSTM's 4× and the GRU's 3× come from their gate counts (3.4, 3.5); the transformer block's 12d² comes from four attention matrices of d² and an FFN of 8d² — so a transformer layer is **three times** an LSTM layer at the same width, and most of that difference is the feed-forward network.

d.title: The honest summary
d.caption: Transformers won on text and are not automatically right elsewhere. On a small tabular problem or a short univariate series, a simpler model is usually better and always cheaper — and on images a modernised CNN matches a vision transformer (2.3), which suggests much of the advantage was the training recipe rather than attention.

d.title: The sentiment data, and the one decision that shapes everything after
d.caption: Vocabulary and sequence length are chosen before any model exists, and both are irreversible in effect: a 10,000-word vocabulary maps everything rarer to `<unk>`, and truncating at 200 tokens discards the end of every longer review — which matters because sentiment is often concluded at the end. Both choices should be made from the data's own length distribution rather than from habit.

nodes.label: Truncate or pad to a fixed length
The end of long reviews is lost
Choose both from the length histogram

d.title: Scaling, and the leak next to it
d.caption: The leak here is a specific and common one: fitting the tokeniser's **vocabulary** on the whole dataset before splitting. The vocabulary is a fitted object like a scaler — it encodes which words exist, which is information from the test set — and the effect is small but real, and entirely avoidable by building it from the training split alone.

nodes.label: Same rule as any scaler
nodes.sub: a fitted object belongs in the fold

nodes.label: The effect is small but real

d.title: The sentiment model, layer by layer
d.caption: Four layers and one shape question. The embedding holds most of the parameters — 10,000 × 128 is 1.28 million against the LSTM's 200 thousand — so this model is mostly a lookup table, and its regularisation should be aimed there first.

d.title: Reading the results, and what to compare against
d.caption: A sentiment accuracy means nothing without the two reference points below it. The majority-class baseline is the floor; a TF-IDF plus logistic regression is the **real** competitor, and on short-text binary sentiment it is frequently within a point or two of an LSTM at a fraction of the cost — which is the ML 11.5 finding, and the reason that comparison belongs in the table.

nodes.label: Often within a point or two
nodes.sub: at a fraction of the cost

nodes.label: So justify the LSTM, or do not use it

d.title: Does scaling matter here?
d.caption: No — and the reason is worth stating, because it is the one case in this course where the answer is a flat no. The input is **token indices**, which are looked up in an embedding table rather than multiplied by a weight; index 9,999 is not 'larger' than index 1 in any sense the model can see. Scaling them would be meaningless, and scaling the embeddings themselves is what LayerNorm is for.

d.title: The setup: four architectures, one task, everything else held
d.caption: The comparison is only meaningful if the differences are the architectures. Same split, same vocabulary, same sequence length, same optimiser and schedule, same number of epochs and the same early-stopping rule — and the embedding dimension matched, because an architecture given a wider embedding is being given more parameters rather than more ability.

nodes.label: One embedding width
nodes.sub: or it is a parameter comparison

d.title: The first result, and why it was not believed
d.caption: The first run produced an ordering that contradicted the theory, and the course's response is the one worth imitating: **treat a surprising result as a bug report against your own setup** before treating it as a finding. 3.3 had already shown exactly this pattern — an LSTM at chance because of a forget-gate bias — so the prior on 'my setup is wrong' was correctly high.

d.title: Ruling out the obvious, one candidate at a time
d.caption: Each row is a hypothesis with a cheap test attached, and the discipline is to find the test that **distinguishes** rather than the one that is easiest to run. Confirming that the data is fine tells you little; finding a measurement whose outcome differs between two live hypotheses is what ends the argument.

d.caption: A measurement is discriminating when the two hypotheses predict **different** outcomes for it. Here the gradient at the first position separates 'the architecture cannot carry the dependency' from 'the architecture can and something else prevents it' — and the answer was the second, which is what pointed at the initialisation rather than at the design.

d.title: The series and the split, where the order is the data
d.caption: A forecasting split has to be chronological, which rules out the shuffle every other task begins with. The window construction is the part that goes wrong: each training example is a window of past values and a target **after** it, and the windows must be built so that no example's inputs overlap a later example's target period.

nodes.label: Slide a window
nodes.sub: L past steps -> H future steps

nodes.label: A gap at the boundary
nodes.sub: so windows do not straddle it

d.title: Reading the results against the baseline that matters
d.caption: For a series, the only reference point that means anything is the **naive forecast** — repeat the last value. A model that cannot beat it has learned nothing, and on many real series it is a genuinely hard target. Reporting MAE without that comparison is the single most common way a forecasting result overstates itself.

nodes.label: Without it, the number is unreadable

d.title: The leakage test, honestly
d.caption: The test that actually works is **truncation**: rebuild every feature from a history cut short at the forecast time, and compare against the features the pipeline produced. If any value differs, something read forward. It is mechanical, it needs no judgement, and it catches the leaks that reading the code does not.

nodes.label: Features as the pipeline built them

d.title: Forecasting-specific leakage, the five that recur
d.caption: Each of these is invisible in a loss curve and each inflates the backtest. The first is the most common by a wide margin, and the last is the most insidious: a scaler fitted over the whole series has folded the test period's **level** into the training data, so even a perfectly windowed model is reading the future.
